Subject: Post-call: scale recovery & request-queue behavior playbook

Hi Mike / Tara (looping Tara for T&C alignment),

Thanks for the productive call today — wanted to capture the core SLO constraints and the concrete next steps so we don't lose momentum. Summary of the requirements you stated: 

- Latency target: 95th percentile <= 200ms for single-turn text generation up to 64 tokens (streaming enabled).
- Sustained throughput: 200 QPS for conversational endpoints during business hours (US East).
- Burst tolerance: handle spikes up to 1,200 QPS for up to 5 minutes with graceful degradation, and full recovery to baseline capacity within 3 minutes of spike end.
- Concurrency: average concurrent open streams ~ 120, peak simultaneous streams ~ 600.
- Streaming semantics: clients expect incremental token delivery; cannot block until full completion.

Immediate asks we agreed on: 
1) Redwood to produce a short playbook describing how autoscale and warm-pool behavior map to these SLOs (what warm pool size, expected scale-up timeline, queueing/backpressure behavior, and degradation modes).
2) Acme to provide a 48-hour representative traffic trace (anonymized) or a synthetic traffic profile we can use for load testing.
3) Confirm any legal/contract constraints around failover regions and data residency (Tara).

Proposed timeline: share the initial playbook + recommended warm-pool config by EOD Friday (2026-06-18). Run a coordinated spike test the week of 2026-06-23 if your engineering team can provide the test window.

I'll attach a draft mutual action plan (MAP) with those milestones; Grace will sketch the load-test plan. If anything above is incorrect, flag and I'll revise.

Thanks,
Alex Martinez

Alex — thanks, this looks right. A couple clarifications from our side: 

- The 200ms 95p is our customer-facing SLO for the onboarding cohort only; for internal tooling (batch summarization) we can accept higher latency. For the onboarding cohort we prioritize no dropped streams.
- The 1,200 QPS spike number was accidental in the call (we rounded up). The correct expected max burst is 950 QPS, but spikes can be very short (30–90s) and we want fast recovery.
- We do want streaming to be best-effort: clients prefer token-level streaming but will tolerate an initial chunked response if necessary during spikes.

Tara: can you confirm if Acme requires SLA region pinning or if cross-region failover is allowable for disaster recovery? That will affect warm-pool placement.

I'll try to export a 6-hour traffic sample from Friday to get you something sooner than the 48-hour request.

Thanks for the clear summary, Alex. A few technical notes that I'll include in the playbook draft: 

- Warm-pool sizing: to meet 95p 200ms at 200 QPS baseline with our default model shard sizes, we recommend a warm pool equivalent to ~30% of peak baseline capacity. For Acme's numbers that maps to ~60 warm instances (we'll show the math in the doc).
- Scale-up timelines: cold-start to a full burst-capable instance is ~75s in our on-demand path; warm instances can accept traffic immediately. Autoscaling policies should target queue-length thresholds and token-rate signals (we'll include sample HPA-like rules).
- Queueing/backpressure: during sustained oversubscription we recommend a hybrid approach — allow a short FIFO request queue with a per-request TTL of 20s, then shed lowest-priority background jobs. For streaming, partial-token flushing is preferable to full drop.
- Recovery behavior: "graceful recovery" means requests queued during scale-up are served at reduced throughput; we'll model the expected 95p degradation curve for your anticipated spike shapes.

Action items for Redwood (Grace / Alex): generate the playbook doc + load-test plan and run an internal dry run against a synthetic 1,000 QPS 90s spike before the joint test. 
Action items for Acme (Mike / Tara): provide a 6–48 hour traffic sample, confirm region/residency constraints, and nominate an engineering contact for the test window.

I attached a quick CSV template you can fill with your traffic histogram (bucketed by minute) — that will let us invert the queueing model faster.

Grace O'Connor
